title: Verifier-integrated LLM intent-to-configuration pipeline: end-to-end safety and rollback evaluation
abstract: We study whether integrating an automated network verifier into an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline reduces unsafe configuration enactments and improves automatic rollback effectiveness in emulated NetOps scenarios. Following a preregistered paired design (CNSM2026-GVR-AV1-001), we generated a shared candidate configuration per intent using gpt-5-mini and executed three pipelines per task: LLM-only (baseline), LLM+verifier (block-on-violation), and LLM+verifier+automatic-rollback. The confirmatory run used 150 paired tasks (300 episodes) stratified by intent ambiguity (benign / ambiguous / partially-specified). Primary outcome: per-task unsafe-enactment rate. Results: across the 150 confirmatory pairs both baseline and guarded pipelines produced valid (non-violating) configurations for all tasks (150/150; baseline rate = 100.0%, guarded rate = 100.0%); paired difference = 0.0 percentage points (exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0). No infrastructure failures, exclusions, or contaminated tasks were recorded above preregistered thresholds. The observed ceiling performance prevents the preregistered hypothesis from being meaningfully tested; we present failure-mode diagnostics, detailed artifacts, and concrete next-step recommendations. All code, raw logs, and hashes are archived in the execution bundle and referenced in the disclosure.

sections.introduction: Modern NetOps workflows increasingly propose intent-driven configuration generation using large language models (LLMs). While LLMs can synthesize vendor configurations from operator intents, their outputs can produce unsafe or service-disrupting changes if not validated. Prior work emphasises that operational reliability depends on verifier-and-constraint machinery surrounding LLMs rather than the model alone [see surveys and applied systems in recent LLM-for-NetOps literature]. We ask, after an autonomy freeze and preregistration: Does adding an automated verifier (and an automated rollback path) to an LLM intent-to-configuration pipeline reduce unsafe enactments and lower service impact in emblematic emulated tasks? Our contributions: (1) a machine-readable preregistered study design (CNSM2026-GVR-AV1-001) and deterministic execution harness; (2) a paired confirmatory experiment (150 tasks, 300 episodes) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator implementation; (3) a fully archived evidence bundle (model transcripts, validator traces, hashes) and reproducible analysis showing ceiling performance in this benchmark, together with diagnostics and prescriptive recommendations for stronger future evaluation.
sections.related_work: We position this study among three streams: (i) intent-driven and LLM-based network configuration (recent conference/workshop papers and surveys on LLMs for NetOps and intent translation); (ii) generate–validate–repair architectures and verifier-augmented generation for safety in code and configuration domains; and (iii) verification and digital-twin approaches for network change validation. Representative verified sources that informed the preregistration and design include prior intent-to-configuration studies and reviews of LLMs for network operations (preregistered evidence records: https://openalex.org/W7114889968; https://openalex.org/W7155247165; https://openalex.org/W7161354925; Nguyen et al., Intent‐Based Network Configuration Using Large Language Models, 2024, doi:10.1002/nem.2313; and related AIOps/agentic-AI reviews). We verified bibliographic metadata for every cited record used to motivate design choices and comparators.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered study CNSM2026-GVR-AV1-001 before execution. Design: paired-binary confirmatory experiment with three per-intent pipelines derived from the shared-initial-candidate generation semantics. Planned confirmatory task count = 150 (power plan targeted a 15 percentage-point absolute reduction). Task bank: CNSM-AI-NetOps-Intent-Bench-v1 (synthetic RFC1918-based intents stratified into benign, ambiguous, partially-specified). Model and prompts: a single frozen hosted model, gpt-5-mini (model provider recorded as openai_responses). Generation policy: one initial generation call per task (shared candidate) and at most one repair call per task as allowed by the preregistered policy. Verifier and validator: the harness used an implementation recorded as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (the preregistration described an open-source verifier interface; the execution used the validator identified in the artifact bundle). Execution harness: adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; each confirmatory task produced paired episodes (baseline, guarded) executed deterministically. Metrics and analysis: primary estimand = per-task unsafe-enactment rate difference (baseline minus guarded). Primary test: paired McNemar exact two-sided test with Bonferroni-adjusted alpha for the two confirmatory comparisons (per-comparison alpha = 0.025). Secondary estimands: conditional rollback success and time-to-detect/rollback. Missingness, contamination, and retry rules were enforced per the preregistered plan.
sections.results: Execution summary: Start 2026-08-25T18:55:00Z; complete 2026-08-25T19:10:50Z. Episodes executed: 300 (150 paired tasks). Model calls used: 150 (shared-initial generation per task). No failed episodes, no infrastructure-missing episodes, and no preregistered exclusions applied. Confirmatory (primary) outcome: baseline unsafe-enactment rate = 0/150 unsafe = 0% unsafe (reported as baseline success rate 150/150 = 100.0% valid configurations). Guarded pipeline unsafe-enactment rate = 0/150 unsafe = 0% unsafe (guarded success rate 150/150 = 100.0%). Paired contingency table: n11=150 (both safe), n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired estimate (guarded minus baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Confidence interval (paired-bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed=1729) for difference = [0.0, 0.0]. Secondary outcomes: no verifier-detected violations occurred in the confirmatory set; therefore the preregistered secondary tests (rollback success proportion, median time-to-rollback) are not applicable for confirmatory inference and are reported qualitatively in the artifact logs. Contamination and missingness: deterministic detectors flagged zero tasks; the abort rule (>2% contaminated) did not trigger. All raw per-task transcripts, validator traces, and artifact hashes are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json; analysis artifacts with sha256 hashes included). Representative scoring JSON for sample tasks are included in the artifact bundle.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The pipeline produced no unsafe enactments under either condition for the chosen task bank and model configuration. As preregistered, this outcome yields a null paired difference but does not confirm the broader operational hypothesis that verifiers materially reduce unsafe enactments in general. Diagnostic readout from the archived validator traces suggests three plausible explanations: (1) the synthetic intent set (CNSM-AI-NetOps-Intent-Bench-v1) was solvable by the LLM in a validator-acceptable form, creating a ceiling effect; (2) the deterministic validator implementation accepted the generated configurations under the deployed validation rules; (3) single-model, single-prompt shared-candidate semantics reduced cross-condition variability by design. Exploratory questions: EQ1–EQ3 (intent ambiguity modulation, residual failure-mode taxonomy, prompt-sensitivity) remain partially unanswered in confirmatory sense because no violations were produced; the raw logs contain diverse intent examples and parser/validator traces for future targeted probing. Operational implication: a verifier+rollback architecture remains conceptually valuable, but benchmarks must exercise verifier-sensitive failure modes (hard constraints, transient-invariant violations, live-state-dependent invariants) to reveal benefits. Reproducibility: all scripts, raw results, scoring tables, and artifact hashes are provided in the execution bundle.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether an automated verifier plus rollback decreases unsafe LLM-generated network-enactments. On the chosen emulated task bank with gpt-5-mini and the deterministic validator harness, both baseline and guarded pipelines produced validator-acceptable configurations for all confirmatory tasks (150/150). The result is a null paired difference (0.0 percentage points; McNemar p = 1.0). The primary scientific outcome is not evidence that verifiers are unnecessary, but evidence that, in this experimental regime, a ceiling effect prevented the hypothesised benefit from manifesting. We release the full artifact bundle to support stronger follow-up studies: (i) harder, adversarial task banks; (ii) multi-model comparisons; (iii) integration with production-grade verifiers (e.g., Batfish-style tools) and live-state checks; (iv) richer metrics (service-impact traces, staged partial violations, rollback coverage). We recommend future work adopt adversarial and stateful change scenarios to stress verifier boundaries and to measure practical operational gains.

disclosure_statement: This study was performed under the CNSM 2026 Agentic AI Researcher constraints. Human role and pre-lock work: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and supplied the initial master prompt and autonomy boundary; pre-lock collaborative development produced reusable harness components but those pre-lock results were not used as empirical evidence. Autonomy and post-lock scope: after the autonomy lock the AI system autonomously conducted literature review, formulated the research question, generated and froze the preregistration (CNSM2026-GVR-AV1-001), implemented the experiment harness, executed the experiment, ran analysis, drafted and revised the manuscript, performed automated peer-review checks, and finalized artifacts. Models and tooling: experiments used a single hosted model identified as gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses in the execution manifest). The adapter/orchestration family used was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The validator invoked in the execution artifacts is recorded as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (the preregistration discussed using an open-source verifier interface; the execution used the validator implementation recorded in the artifact bundle). Prompting and generation semantics: the exact frozen master prompt and the autonomy-bound instructions are preserved in the archived preregistration and execution bundle (preregistration SHA-256: 66fbf2c56649115c66412326fcc739ebacced84ec2df3fca796f4e7eac4a9b04). The shared_initial_candidate generation policy (one initial generation call per task; at most one repair call per task) was enforced. Experiment preregistration: the full machine-readable preregistration (study_id CNSM2026-GVR-AV1-001) was completed and frozen prior to execution; the preregistration defined hypotheses H1/H2, exploratory questions, sampling, exclusion, retry, contamination, and analysis plans. Execution artifacts and reproducibility: the run produced 300 episodes (150 paired tasks), used 150 model calls, and completed with no failed episodes. All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONL lines, analysis scripts, and artifact hashes are included in the execution bundle (execution_manifest.json and analysis artifacts with sha256 hashes). Peer review and revision: manuscript drafting, review checks (methodological, statistical, novelty, and reference integrity), and revision were performed autonomously per the track rules. Human editing: no manual human editing, rewriting, or selective improvement of technical content was performed after the autonomy lock; the human Research Director did not alter technical manuscript content post-lock. Deviations and restarts: no preregistered deviations were recorded; no manual restarts were performed except automated retry policies for transient provider errors per the preregistration. Limitations of autonomy: pre-lock infrastructure development occurred in collaboration with the Research Director but those pre-lock artifacts were not incorporated as empirical evidence unless recreated under the post-lock pipeline; this run abided by that constraint. Ethical and safety oversight: the study used only synthetic emulated tasks and containerized router images; no real private network data were used. The artifact bundle documents contamination detectors (regex scanners, exact-match fingerprint checks) and their outputs; these detectors are heuristic and cannot guarantee absence of subtle training-data leakage. Contact and artifact access: the full machine-readable preregistration, execution logs, raw transcripts, analysis scripts, and artifact hashes are archived with the study bundle referenced in the manuscript.
limitations: Ceiling effect: all 150 confirmatory tasks produced validator-acceptable configurations under both pipelines; this prevents demonstrating a verifier benefit in this regime.
Synthetic/emulated benchmark: CNSM-AI-NetOps-Intent-Bench-v1 is synthetic and may not exercise real-world, stateful, or adversarial failure modes encountered in production NetOps.
Single-model scope: experiments used one hosted model (gpt-5-mini); results do not generalize across models or model families.

Validator specificity: the execution validator is recorded as deterministic_netops_validator_v5; its acceptance criteria and coverage may differ from other verifiers (e.g., Batfish) and from live-system invariants.

Sample size and scenario diversity: although powered per preregistration for a sizable absolute reduction, the absence of observed violations limits inferential conclusions; richer adversarial or stateful scenarios are needed.
Contamination detection limits: deterministic detectors flagged zero contaminated tasks but cannot rule out subtle training-data leakage not detectable by exact- or regex-based scans.

Construct validity: the primary metric (unsafe-enactment as detected by the validator) depends on the validator rules; it is an imperfect proxy for some operational harms (transient service degradation, timing-related outages, or side effects not encoded in validator rules).
